questions.question_text: Which of the following authors or auth or teams was the first to place the therapist in the active role?

options.text: Sigmund Freud.
Albert Ellis.
Franz Alexander and Thomas French.
Milton Erickson.
Aaron Beck.

questions.explanation: Although Sigmund Freud saw patients with short-term cases, brief therapy arguably dates back to the publication of Alexander and French’s (1946) Psychoanalytic Therapy: Principles and Applications. While Ellis, Erickson, and Beck have all contributed significantly to brief work, it is Alexander and French who first formally placed the therapist in the active role of promoting patient health and who argued that change was not primarily a function of insight but of experience. Research has gone on to support the usefulness of this more active approach.

questions.question_text: In contrast to the historic role of the psychoanalyst as a 'blank screen,' brief therapists use which of the following strategies?

options.text: Accepting all forbidden and objectionable responses of patients.
Actively collaborating with the patient to achieve therapeutic goals.
Refraining from allowing the therapist's personality to influence the real relationship between therapist and patient.
Focusing on insight rather than experience.
Keeping the focus on self-exploration.

correct_answer.text: Actively collaborating with the patient to achieve therapeutic goals.

correct_answers.text: Actively collaborating with the patient to achieve therapeutic goals.

questions.explanation: Although Freud saw patients with short-term cases, brief therapy arguably dates back to the publication of Alexander and French’s (1946) classic work Psychoanalytic Therapy: Principles and Applications. They were the first to formally place the therapist in the active role of promoting patient health. Change, they argued, was not primarily a function of insight but of experience. Therefore, the therapist’s role was to foster “corrective emotional experiences.” These are replays of previous conflicted situations that end more positively within the helping relationship. This reformulation took therapists out of their historic role as “blank screens” and cast them as active treatment agents who could use their relationships with patients to catalyze needed developmental experiences. Research has gone on to support the usefulness of this more active approach. Lengthy treatments, which associated therapeutic gains primarily with the attainment of patient insights, have not turned out to be as central to change as many psychoanalysts assumed (Fisher and Greenberg 1996). With the writings of Peter Sifneos (1972), James Mann (1973), David Malan (1976), and Habib Davanloo (1980), brevity has become an accepted part of the psychoanalytic lexicon. The rise of behavior therapies contributed significantly to the prominence of brief work. Behavioral treatments cast the therapist in the role of teacher. No longer was therapy about self-exploration. Rather, it was intended to teach coping skills and alter learned action patterns. This permitted therapy to be highly circumscribed, emphasizing directive teaching and structured homework assignments between sessions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered an important task for the patient in cognitive reprocessing therapy?

options.text: Develop insight into drives.
Identify and test negative thoughts.
Foster inflexible patterns of thought and behavior.
Rehearse old cognitive and behavioral responses.
Work through transference issues.

questions.explanation: According to the approach used in cognitive reprocessing therapies, symptoms can be traced to automatic thought patterns that distort information processing and produce negative thoughts about self, others, and the future (cognitive triad). The goal of therapy is to identify these thought patterns, challenge them, and replace them with more constructive alternatives (J.S. Beck 1995). Developing insight into one’s drives and working through transference issues are not considered important or necessary tasks in cognitive reprocessing therapies

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapeutic strategies is likely to be employed during a brief psychodynamic therapy session?

options.text: The therapist emphasizes that change cannot occur until patients develop full insight into their drives.
The therapist focuses on historical patterns within the therapeutic relationship.
The therapist takes a passive role in the therapeutic process.
The therapist involves him- or herself in the core conflictual relationship patterns.
The therapist uses interpretation as the chief therapeutic tool.

correct_answer.text: The therapist involves him- or herself in the core conflictual relationship patterns.

correct_answers.text: The therapist involves him- or herself in the core conflictual relationship patterns.

questions.explanation: Although psychodynamic brief therapies retain the theoretical and conceptual heritage of psychoanalysis, there are some important operational modifications. Brief dynamic therapists do not rely on interpretation, lengthy exploration of the past, or the development of insight as necessary sources of change. Change is catalyzed by the involvement of the therapist in core relationship patterns, breaking the cycles of repetition by providing responses different from those anticipated by patients (Levenson 1995). By limiting the work to a circumscribed “here and now” focus and being active in the therapeutic process, short-term psychodynamic therapy can accelerate the rate of change and decrease the number of treatment sessions (Luborsky and Mark 1991).

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies is not available in manualized form?

options.text: Cognitive-behavioral therapy.
Dialectical behavioral therapy.
Interpersonal therapy.
Solution-focused brief therapy.
Strategic brief therapy.

questions.explanation: Strategic brief therapy has not yet been manualized.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be a standard element of the learning model intrinsic to behavioral (exposure-based) therapies and cognitive reprocessing therapies?

options.text: Psychoeducation about how and why symptoms appear.
Active practice of techniques.
Out-of-session homework.
Free association.
Relaxation training.

questions.explanation: Free association is not typically a core therapeutic ingredient of the learning therapies and is usually employed in psychoanalytic or psychodynamic treatments. In the learning model of treatment, the presenting concerns of patients are viewed as learned maladaptive patterns that can be unlearned. Moreover, patients are seen as capable of acquiring new, adaptive patterns of thought and action through skill development. As a result, the learning therapies feature the therapist in an active, directive teaching mode and the patient as a student. This structuring of the helping relationship lends itself to active skill rehearsal within sessions and directed homework between meetings. Treatment typically begins with a period of assessment and psychosocial education explaining how and why symptoms appear. Specific skills are taught, such as relaxation designed to help control symptoms. The combination of a tight learning focus and active practice of techniques ensures that most learning therapies are short term by their very nature. The learning therapies can be separated into two types: 1) behavioral treatments that emphasize exposure as a central therapeutic ingredient, and 2) cognitive reprocessing therapies that more broadly target dysfunctional patterns of information processing for restructuring

questions.question_text: In a couple's treatment, the husband voices concerns about rejection from his wife and tends to avoid intimate interactions with her. Which of the following would be a reason for the therapist to use solution-focused brief therapy?

options.text: The problem is clearly a result of only one party.
The couple is invested in exploring childhood and formative experiences.
The husband is interested in a formulation of his personality.
The husband can identify problem-free areas of his life where the symptom does not occur.
The couple has multiple presenting concerns.

correct_answer.text: The husband can identify problem-free areas of his life where the symptom does not occur.

correct_answers.text: The husband can identify problem-free areas of his life where the symptom does not occur.

questions.explanation: Solution-focused brief therapists start from the premise that people are changing all the time, enacting solution patterns as well as problem ones (Ratner et al. 2012). Indeed, there is an important sense in this therapy in which problems do not exist at all. When patients cannot reach their goals, they at some point identify that they have a problem. This reification becomes self-fulfilling: the more patients focus on their problems, the more troubled they feel and act. Equally important, such a problem focus blinds patients to the occasions in which they do, in fact, reach their goals. The aim of solution-focused brief therapy is to break this self-fulfilling conceptualization. The therapist accomplishes this by focusing on solution patterns rather than on problems. Thus, in the initial assessment therapists ask patients to identify positive pre-session changes and occasions during which problems either do not occur or occur less often or less intensely (Walter and Peller 1992). Enacting these exceptions to problem patterns—doing more of what is already working (de Shazer 1988; O’Hanlon and Weiner-Davis 1989)— is the focus of therapy, not an analysis of core conflicts or a teaching of skills to remediate deficits. Because the therapy is not initiating new behavior and thought patterns but instead is building on existing ones, it tends to be highly targeted, lasting several sessions on average (Steenbarger 2012).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about characteristics shared by the brief psychotherapies is true?

options.text: The brief therapies are similar in scope and duration.
All of the brief therapies stress in-session experience as central to change.
All of the brief therapies are manualized.
All of the brief therapies set limits on the number of sessions at the outset of treatment.
In all brief therapies, it is the therapist who maintains the treatment focus from session to session.

correct_answer.text: In all brief therapies, it is the therapist who maintains the treatment focus from session to session.

correct_answers.text: In all brief therapies, it is the therapist who maintains the treatment focus from session to session.

questions.explanation: Brief therapies can be conceptualized along a continuum, ranging from highly abbreviated and highly structured contextual therapies to more exploratory relational treatments. The major schools of brief therapy differ in scope, degree of structure, use of time in treatment, and nature of the therapist activity, but as a group it is the therapist who maintains the treatment focus from session to session

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best reflects how presenting problems are viewed in strategic therapy?

options.text: The presenting concerns of patients are acquired over a brief period of time.
Problems are not an artifact of person-situation interactions but rather emanate from within the patient.
Presenting concerns are the result of attempts at solutions that reinforce the initial problem.
Fundamental changes in personality must occur before the presenting problems can be addressed in therapy.
The therapist's role is to find a solution for the patient's problem.

correct_answer.text: Presenting concerns are the result of attempts at solutions that reinforce the initial problem.

correct_answers.text: Presenting concerns are the result of attempts at solutions that reinforce the initial problem.

questions.explanation: Strategic therapies, including single-session treatments (Hoyt et al. 1992), view presenting concerns as the result of attempts at solutions that unwittingly reinforce the very problems patients are attempting to address (Rosenbaum 1990). A person concerned about rejection in relationships, for instance, might interact in guarded ways, leading others to avoid future interaction. The problem, from the vantage point of the strategic therapist, is a function of the patient’s construal of the situation and the ways in which that construal are reinforced through social interaction (Quick 2008). As Rosenbaum (1990) emphasized, the goal of the therapy is not to find a solution for a patient’s problem but to create a situation that lends itself to spontaneous goal attainment. By changing the patient’s context—from being stuck in a pattern to enacting a strength—the therapist allows naturally occurring growth processes to take their own course. In that sense, strategic therapy is a process for removing barriers to change and not a self-contained change process in itself.

questions.question_text: Which of the following patient variables predicts the need for a longer course of treatment or additional maintenance sessions?

options.text: Chronic emotional and behavioral patterns.
Simple presenting problems.
Lack of comorbid substance abuse.
Patients in precontemplative stages of change.
Strong social supports.

questions.explanation: Findings from early investigations of the dose-effect relation in psychotherapy suggest that much of therapy’s effect occurs in a brief period for a large proportion of patients. It also indicates that some patients benefit from more extended treatment. In general, patients who begin treatment at higher levels of psychological functioning require fewer sessions (Lambert 2013; Lambert and Ogles 2004). Patient selection criteria forming the acronym DISCUS can be useful during initial interviews in determining the likelihood that treatment changes will be achieved briefly. These criteria focus on the following areas: Duration of presenting problems, Interpersonal functioning, Severity of presenting problems, Complexity of presenting problems, Understanding of the need for change, and Social supports.
